paper.title: Sibling Spillovers
paper.code_data_availability: The authors were granted an exemption to publish their data because access to the data is restricted. …

registers.role: sample frame; birth order; birth outcomes; linkage to parents and siblings
treatment (disability diagnoses of the third child); hospital use

variables_mentioned: 9th grade exit exam grade point average

registers.role: controls and descriptive statistics on parents
sample frame; birth order; birth outcomes; alternative treatment (health problems at birth)
outcomes (FCAT test scores, grades 3–8); treatment (primary disability category); 1st grade school quality
variables_mentioned: Florida Comprehensive Assessment Test (FCAT) maths and reading scores

linkages: Denmark: 'A unique identification number enables us to link children to their parents and siblings' and to match birth records to other administrative registers
Florida: 'Florida's education and health agencies matched children along three dimensions: first and last names, date of birth and social security number'
families are required to have at least three observed births and the same father on the birth certificate for the first two children

sample.universe: all singletons born in Florida between 1994 and 2002 and subsequently educated in Florida public schools; all births in Denmark between 1990 and 2001
sample.unit_of_observation: child (child–year for the pooled Florida FCAT observations in grades 3–8; one observation per child in Denmark); two children — the first- and second-born — per family
selection_rules: at least three births observed in the family (Florida) / the first three children observed (Denmark)
the father is the same for the first two births
only the first two births enter the estimation sample; third-borns are excluded
Florida: singletons born 1994–2002 and educated in Florida public schools; each pair of children observed at least in grade 3 and in every subsequent grade used
Denmark: births 1990–2001; birth outcomes observed only for children born from 1994 forward
no restrictions imposed on the disability status of the first two children
sample.n_observations: 104,130 child–year observations in Florida; 57,162 children in Denmark
sample.n_individuals: 9,812 Florida families and 28,581 Danish families in the estimation sample; 9,987 Florida and 28,581 Danish three-plus-child families in the descriptive sample, of which 2,483 Florida and 1,882 Danish families have a third child observed with a disability by age 5

construction_notes: outcome variables are cohort-standardised to mean zero and standard deviation one and combine maths and reading assessments
Florida FCAT observations are pooled across grades 3–8 to reduce measurement error; the average grade in the Florida data set is 5.3 and the median is 5

disability in Florida is the single primary disability recorded in mutually exclusive categories on the school record; in Denmark it is diagnoses recorded in the medical registries, which are not mutually exclusive
asthma is not counted as a disability (footnote 9)
treatment is defined on the third child and measured by age 5, between ages 5 and 10, or by age 10
birth outcomes are missing for 9.1% of Danish observations; zero is imputed and an indicator for the missing value is included
the alternative treatment is a congenital anomaly or abnormal condition at birth (Florida only), birth weight below 2,500 g, gestational age below 37 weeks, or a five-minute Apgar score below 6
low birth weight is defined as birth weight under 2,500 g; Apgar scores are observed on a ten-point scale
maternal education is measured at the time of the first sibling's birth
exposure is measured either by birth order (second- vs first-born) or by the difference in years of exposure to the third child
standard errors are adjusted for clustering at the family level throughout

links.pointer_quote: The magnitude of these differences is significant; for example, in Florida it is about half of the observed relationship between an extra year of maternal education and children's test scores.
These results are concentrated in cases in which the third-child's disability is observed early—and therefore, presumably, more likely to affect older siblings in early childhood.

claims.statement: In Florida, the second-born ('more exposed') child's test scores fall relative to the first-born's when the third child is observed disabled by age 5, in a family fixed-effects difference-in-differences model with birth order (second-born vs first-born) as the exposure measure (Table 3, Panel A, column 1).

treatment.label: Third child observed disabled by age 5, interacted with being second-born ('more exposed')

register_source.value: Florida school records (primary disability category) / Danish medical patient register diagnoses; the birth-problem treatment is taken from the birth certificate / Danish Birth Register

definition.value: Indicator D for the third-born child being observed with a disability by age 5 (the primary disability category in Florida school records at kindergarten entry; diagnoses in the Danish medical patient register), interacted with the indicator M for being second-born rather than first-born; β2 on D×M is the parameter of interest

timing.value: Disability of the third-born child measured by age 5; exposure accumulates from the third child's birth until the older siblings' outcomes are measured

outcome.label: Test scores (Florida Comprehensive Assessment Test, FCAT)

register_source.value: Florida school records (FCAT), matched to Florida birth records

definition.value: The state's criterion-referenced end-of-year standardised test (FCAT), administered in grades 3–8, cohort-standardised to mean zero and standard deviation one; the outcome combines maths and reading assessments and a child's observations are pooled across grades 3–8

timing.value: grades 3–8 (average grade 5.3, median 5), i.e. elementary and middle school, after the third child's birth

units.value: standard deviations of the cohort-standardised outcome

estimand.target_population: first- and second-born children in families with at least three observed births (same father for the first two) in which the third child is observed with a disability
estimand.formal_query: β2 = {E[Y | second-born, disabled third child] − E[Y | first-born, disabled third child]} − {E[Y | second-born, non-disabled third child] − E[Y | first-born, non-disabled third child]}

population.description: Florida singletons born 1994–2002 and subsequently educated in Florida public schools, in families in which at least three births are observed and the father is the same on the birth certificate for the first two children; only the first- and second-born children enter the estimation sample
population.ages: test scores measured in grades 3–8 (average grade 5.3, median 5)
subgroups_defined: mother college graduate / complete high school or some college / high school dropout (or basic school only)
third child's disability observed by age 5 vs between ages 5 and 10
physical vs cognitive or behavioural disabilities
immigrant vs native-born mothers
maternal grandmother in the same municipality (Denmark)
disability severity (Florida)
population.selection: families with at least three observed births and the same father on the birth certificate for the first two children; children matched from birth records to Florida public-school records; third-borns excluded from the estimation sample

identification.source_of_variation: differential exposure of the first- and second-born child to a disabled third-born sibling, arising from birth order (and in columns 4–6 from birth spacing), differenced against the same birth-order gap in families whose third child is not disabled; family fixed effects absorb time-invariant family differences

key_assumptions.assumption: Common (parallel) trends: in the absence of the third child's disability there are no differential trends between families with and without a disabled third child
key_assumptions.supported_by: no difference-in-differences 'effects' on birth outcomes of the first two children (Table 4), on time-varying family characteristics (Table 5), and no relationship between third-child disability and predetermined characteristics interacted with birth order (Table 6 F-tests)

key_assumptions.assumption: The effect of birth order does not vary with the presence of a disabled third sibling other than through the differential exposure to that sibling
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors state they cannot test this directly, and instead run placebo difference-in-differences on outcomes predetermined relative to the third child's birth

key_assumptions.assumption: Family fixed effects net out the time-invariant differences between families with and without a disabled third child
key_assumptions.supported_by: descriptive comparison of families with and without a disabled third child (Table 1, columns 4–6), which motivates the within-family design

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on being a family with at least three observed births and the same father for the first two births
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors describe this as a limitation of the design and re-estimate the models weighting three-plus-child families by the characteristics of two-child families (Online Appendix Table B1)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: parents do not act on an anticipated disability of the third child (e.g. selective abortion) in ways that change family composition
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors state they are unable to address this empirically but note that third-child disability is not correlated with subsequent fertility or family size (Online Appendix Table B14)

key_assumptions.assumption: The third child's disability classification is not endogenously determined by the older siblings' school performance (no co-diagnosis / reverse causality)
key_assumptions.supported_by: replication using health problems recorded at the time of birth as an alternative treatment (Table 7) and re-estimation on families in which neither of the first two children is observed as disabled (Online Appendix Table B12)

threats_discussed: families with disabled third children may already have been trending differently before the third birth
selective abortion in anticipation of a disabled child (footnote 15)
endogenous identification or co-diagnosis: the third child's disability might be recorded because an older sibling performs poorly
differential family size due to endogenous fertility
three-child families are not representative of all families (external validity)
robustness_checks: placebo difference-in-differences on predetermined birth outcomes: birth weight, ln(birth weight), low birth weight, five-minute Apgar score (Table 4)
placebo difference-in-differences on time-varying family characteristics: zip-code income, 1st grade school quality, marital status, paternal and maternal income (Table 5)
regression of third-child disability on predetermined characteristics interacted with second-born status, with joint F-tests (Table 6)
alternative treatment: the third child's health problems recorded at birth (Table 7)
exposure measured in years of birth spacing instead of birth order (Table 3, columns 4–6)
controls for birth outcomes, and for marital status and income (Table 3, columns 2–3 and 5–6)
Florida families with at least five years' spacing between the second and third birth: differential probability that the second-born is identified as disabled before the third birth
re-estimation weighting three-plus-child families by the characteristics of two-child families (Online Appendix Table B1)
re-estimation on families in which neither the first- nor the second-born child is observed as disabled (Online Appendix Table B12)
single-grade estimates instead of pooling grades 3–8 in Florida
treating asthma as a disability (footnote 9)
hospital use of the first two children at ages 1 and 2, and maternal employment at child age 1 or 2, in Denmark (Online Appendix Tables B10 and B11)
unresolved_confounders: unobserved differences between families with and without a disabled child, which prevent the authors from estimating the total (as opposed to relative) effect of exposure to a disabled sibling
the common-trends assumption cannot be tested directly
1st grade school quality in Florida is measured after the third child's birth for most families and can be thought of as endogenous to the third child's disability labelling (footnote 24)

estimator.value: OLS difference-in-differences with family fixed effects

estimation.specification: equation (1): family fixed effects, the second-born indicator and its interaction with third-child disability; exposure measured by birth order (second-born vs first-born)

source_table.value: Table 3, Panel A, first row (3rd observed disabled by age 5), column (1)

heterogeneity.dimension: timing of the third child's disability
heterogeneity.finding: the spillover is concentrated in disabilities observed by age 5; the differential for disabilities first observed between ages 5 and 10 is a small fraction of it and far from statistically significant (Table 3)
deleterious effects are found only for physical disabilities, not for cognitive or behavioural ones (Online Appendix Table B2)

U-shaped in Florida (most negative at the bottom and the top of the SES distribution); in Denmark no negative spillover at the top but negative in the lower two groups; equality of coefficients cannot be rejected (p = 0.45 Florida, p = 0.14 Denmark) (Table 8)
estimates are more negative for immigrant mothers in both settings (−0.066 vs −0.042 in Florida; −0.119 vs −0.015 in Denmark), though not statistically significantly so (Online Appendix Table B18)

the negative effects are driven by parents living in a different municipality from the maternal grandmother, or by families where grandmaternal care is not available at all (Online Appendix Table B17)
effects are most negative when the third child has a moderately severe disability, relative to mild or very severe disabilities (Online Appendix Table B13)
larger effects on reading than mathematics in Florida; larger for mathematics than reading in Denmark, neither statistically significant (Online Appendix Table B4)

index_sets.over: individuals; i = 1, 2, i.e. the first- and second-born child only
families

value.normalisation: Y normalised to have mean zero and standard deviation one within cohort; M = 0 (first-born, 'less exposed') is the reference category; the level indicator for third-child disability D is not identified because it is constant across the first two births

value.claimed_domain: how families function more broadly — spillovers and dynamics within the family, as opposed to something very context-specific
boundary_conditions: estimated only for families with three or more children, which the authors state are not representative of all families
measures the effect of relative, not total, exposure to a disabled sibling

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: Our paper builds on this work, and is the first to examine the effects of sibling disability status on the educational success of other children using within-family design.
using Norwegian data, Rege et al. (2011) estimate detrimental effects of about 5% to 6% of a standard deviation which is similar to our main effects

falsification.condition: difference-in-differences 'effects' on outcomes of the first two children that were predetermined relative to the third child's birth would be interpreted as an indication of confoundedness

outcomes_examined_not_reported: maternal and paternal labour supply estimated with the preferred difference-in-differences strategy (footnote 29 states only that there are no economically meaningful or statistically significant differential effects; no estimates are printed)

anchor_quote.text: The paper finds evidence that, relative to the first born, the second child in a family is differentially affected when the third child is disabled.

links.pointer_quote: Specifically, we observe that, in both Denmark and Florida, the second-born child in a family has worse outcomes (test scores in Florida, grade point average in Denmark) than does his or her older sibling when the third-born sibling is disabled, relative to the case in which the third-born sibling is not disabled.
These results are concentrated in cases in which the third-child's disability is observed early—and therefore, presumably, more likely to affect older siblings in early childhood.

key_assumptions.supported_by: descriptive comparison of families with and without a disabled third child (Table 1, columns 4–6), which motivates the within-family design

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on being a family with at least three observed births and the same father for the first two births
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors describe this as a limitation of the design and re-estimate the models weighting three-plus-child families by the characteristics of two-child families (Online Appendix Table B1)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: parents do not act on an anticipated disability of the third child (e.g. selective abortion) in ways that change family composition
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors state they are unable to address this empirically but note that third-child disability is not correlated with subsequent fertility or family size (Online Appendix Table B14)

key_assumptions.assumption: The third child's disability classification is not endogenously determined by the older siblings' school performance (no co-diagnosis / reverse causality)
key_assumptions.supported_by: replication using health problems recorded at the time of birth as an alternative treatment (Table 7) and re-estimation on families in which neither of the first two children is observed as disabled (Online Appendix Table B12)

threats_discussed: families with disabled third children may already have been trending differently before the third birth
selective abortion in anticipation of a disabled child (footnote 15)
endogenous identification or co-diagnosis: the third child's disability might be recorded because an older sibling performs poorly
differential family size due to endogenous fertility
three-child families are not representative of all families (external validity)
robustness_checks: placebo difference-in-differences on predetermined birth outcomes: birth weight, ln(birth weight), low birth weight, five-minute Apgar score (Table 4)
placebo difference-in-differences on time-varying family characteristics: zip-code income, 1st grade school quality, marital status, paternal and maternal income (Table 5)
regression of third-child disability on predetermined characteristics interacted with second-born status, with joint F-tests (Table 6)
alternative treatment: the third child's health problems recorded at birth (Table 7)
exposure measured in years of birth spacing instead of birth order (Table 3, columns 4–6)
controls for birth outcomes, and for marital status and income (Table 3, columns 2–3 and 5–6)
Florida families with at least five years' spacing between the second and third birth: differential probability that the second-born is identified as disabled before the third birth
re-estimation weighting three-plus-child families by the characteristics of two-child families (Online Appendix Table B1)
re-estimation on families in which neither the first- nor the second-born child is observed as disabled (Online Appendix Table B12)
single-grade estimates instead of pooling grades 3–8 in Florida
treating asthma as a disability (footnote 9)
hospital use of the first two children at ages 1 and 2, and maternal employment at child age 1 or 2, in Denmark (Online Appendix Tables B10 and B11)
